task_text: Fix merge_intervals(intervals) in solution.py. Inputs are lists of [start,end] integer CLOSED intervals. Merge overlaps AND touching endpoints, sort by start, return fresh list-of-lists, never mutate input (including inner lists). Empty list returns[]. Reversed interval start>end raises ValueError before producing a result. Degenerate [x,x] is valid. No imports or dependencies. Return full solution.py in files, with only pure functions; allowed built-ins len/range/enumerate/zip/sorted/list/tuple/str/int/float/bool/abs/min/max/sum/round/ValueError; the only allowed method call is list.append. Do not include tests. Inputs have at most12 intervals with coordinates -20..20.

fixed: Replaced in-place intervals.sort() (mutates caller's list) with sorted() over freshly copied [start,end] lists
Changed merge condition from strict '<' to '<=' so touching endpoints (e.g. [1,2] and [2,3]) merge
Fixed merge to take max(existing_end, new_end) instead of overwriting with new end, so contained intervals like [2,3] inside [1,4] don't shrink the range
Added validation that raises ValueError when start > end for any interval, checked before building/returning any result
answer.behavior: merge_intervals now validates all intervals, copies them (never touching input), sorts by start, merges overlapping or touching closed intervals using max end, and returns a fresh list of fresh inner lists

response.concise_method_summary: Rewrote merge_intervals to: (1) iterate input once, unpack each pair, raise ValueError immediately if start>end, and append a new [start,end] list to a fresh 'copies' list (input is never read into by reference nor mutated); (2) produce 'ordered = sorted(copies)', which sorts lexicographically by start then end using only the sorted() builtin (no .sort() method call, no lambda); (3) merge by scanning ordered pairs, starting a new merged interval unless the current start is <= the last merged interval's end (this makes touching endpoints merge, e.g. [1,2]+[2,3] -> [1,3]), and when merging, set merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end) via a plain if-comparison and index assignment (not a method call) so a fully-contained interval like [2,3] inside [1,4] doesn't shrink the merged end; (4) return merged, a brand-new list of brand-new two-element lists. Only builtins used: len is unused but allowed set includes sorted, list (implicit via literals), and the single permitted method call list.append. Empty input short-circuits naturally to an empty merged list. No imports, no comprehensions with disallowed calls, no docstring, no tests in the file.
assumptions: Each inner list in intervals has exactly two integers [start, end]; no length validation is performed since the spec only requires handling start>end

Sorting the copied [start,end] pairs lexicographically via plain sorted() satisfies 'sort by start' (ties on start are broken by end, which is a reasonable default and doesn't violate any stated requirement)
Touching endpoints means one interval's end equals another's start for closed intervals, so start <= previous_end is the correct merge trigger

Raising ValueError as soon as the first invalid interval (start>end) is encountered, before any copying/sorting/merging of later data is 'produced', satisfies 'raises ValueError before producing a result'
list literal construction ([start, end]) and tuple unpacking (start, end = iv[0], iv[1]) are not considered disallowed method calls under the stated constraints
Degenerate intervals [x,x] pass validation (x>x is False) and merge correctly with adjacent touching intervals
proposed_verification: merge_intervals([[1,4],[2,3]]) == [[1,4]]  # containment doesn't shrink end (max logic)
merge_intervals([[3,1]]) raises ValueError, and calling with [[3,1],[1,2]] also raises without mutating the input
x=[[2,1],[1,2]]; try/except around merge_intervals(x) then assert x == [[2,1],[1,2]] and merge_intervals([]) == []  # input untouched, empty case handled
